title: Industrial relations: Unions strike deals on bargaining, AI, lockouts
full_text:
Unions have committed Labor to extending the reach of same job, same pay laws, increase their ability to force employers into collective bargaining, introduce new powers to restrict employer lockouts, and consider more time off due to gains from artificial intelligence.
Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth strongly backed the amendments to the party platform at the Labor national conference on Friday and told delegates in Adelaide that they committed the Albanese government to amend the Fair Work Act.
Employers have accused unions of seeking to boost their power while denying employers their defence.
Meanwhile, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association moved a resolution calling on the Albanese government to "engage with unions and employers to examine how a 'time dividend' can be returned to Australian workers".
SDA NSW secretary Bernie Smith claimed workers had not shared in the 15 per cent productivity growth over the last 20 years and warned artificial intelligence may see even greater productivity rises in the next decade.
"If you want workers to engage in an AI revolution, they need to see a down payment now," he told delegates. "That could be five weeks' annual leave, it could be a shorter working week or, as they say in the taco ad, maybe we could have both."
As revealed by The Australian Financial Review, unions moved amendments to restrict employers' ability to lock out workers by ensuring lockouts cannot be longer than the worker stoppages they respond to.
The amendment - delayed until Saturday but not opposed - commits Labor to "amend the Fair Work Act to empower workers and their unions to apply to the Fair Work Commission for an order to suspend disproportionate employer response action".
Unions have argued disproportionate lockouts, some lasting months, have become routine in mining.
Flagging her support, Rishworth told delegates that locking out workers for weeks or months "is not fair, and that is why the amendment will commit a Labor government to put a stop to it".
ACTU secretary Sally McManus told the conference there was "no clearer example of abuse of power of multinationals trampling over ordinary Australians and regional communities than locking workers out for months to starve them into submission".
Minerals Council chief executive Tania Constable said, "this is yet another attempt by unions to encourage the government to increase union powers over employers at every opportunity, while denying businesses the right to defend themselves wherever they can".
The Mining and Energy Union moved amendments to limit a trainee exclusion in the government's same job, same pay laws, which require labour hire workers to be paid the same as direct employees.
The MEU claimed that labour hire companies were abusing the exemption by classifying labour hire workers as trainees - even when training may be minimal or incidental - to avoid paying the higher rate.
It clashes with a recent statutory review of the laws, by former Fair Work commissioner Susan Booth, which specifically rejected the change as it was concerned it "may have implications for participation in training pathways that contribute to Australia's future skills needs".
Rishworth said Labor was "committed to act against any efforts to undermine our groundbreaking same job, same pay reforms". The SDA passed platform changes to extend powers that let unions unilaterally start enterprise bargaining to multi-employer agreements.
The current powers are triggered for bargaining to replace agreements that expired in the past five years. Once bargaining is initiated, workers can take industrial action.
Over the past year, the SDA has won landmark orders to start bargaining multi-employer agreements with McDonald's and Chemist Warehouse.
SDA South Australia secretary Josh Peak, who praised the Albanese government as "the most pro-worker and pro-union government we have seen in a generation", said unions could not afford to lose gains won through bargaining by employers who did not want to bargain.
The amendment commits Labor to alter the act to ensure that the trainee exclusion can only apply when an employee is undertaking "genuine training", and to consider potentially removing other exclusions to the laws.
On Friday, Rishworth said she would move an amendment to clamp down on "sham unions", which she defined as unions that were not registered under union regulation laws.
These include the Retail and Fast Food Workers Union, a left-wing rival to the dominant SDA, or so-called red unions such as the Nurses' Professional Association of Queensland.
